catalog_quote: Kondic 2012:48: "1.2 Stress The main lexical HSF stress is regular, and commonly falls on the (first) long vowel (HSF stress seems to be attracted by a heavy syllable). If there is no long vowel in a word, then the accent is on the first short vowel. This rule has already been proposed by Larsen and Pike (1949) for San Luis Potosí Huastec. ['?uxum] uxum woman [manu'nu:l] manunuul yellow [ta'ta:?] tataa' you, 2sg ['tamup] tamup year ... In South Eastern Huastec two long vowels normally do not occur in one word. ... The personal markers that precede a verbal complex are never stressed. They are written separately from the word in order to show that they do not interfere with the stress rule." sweep_summary: One title-works with stress in the title for Huastec: Hagberg 1993/2006, An autosegmental theory of stress (Glottolog 141035; the 2006 SIL e-Books 3 reissue of the 1993 Arizona dissertation). The full text was already held by the project in this reading (archive.org item an-autosegmental-theory-of-stress, in the capa1241 folder) and was copied into with a extracted text layer and a line; PDF pages 199-200 were viewed as images to verify the accent marks. Hagberg treats Huastec (Larsen & Pike 1949 data, Potosino) as unbounded quantity-sensitive: stress on the rightmost long vowel, else the first vowel (WSP right-to-left + End Rule Left, no feet, word domain), with 12 forms in (82). This confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding and the rightmost-long-vowel reading the catalog the primary-stress rule already carries for Potosino; it is second-hand, so it does not supersede Kondic 2012:48 as the deciding first-hand source. Its rendering of Larsen & Pike ('rightmost' long vowel) differs from Kondic's '(first) long vowel' attribution to the same paper, which the catalog already notes as a partial disagreement. Nothing from this item remains to be acquired; the primary Larsen & Pike 1949 (JSTOR 10.2307/410088) is still paywalled by automated download per the earlier. The MPI handle landing page (pure.mpg.de item_401934) could not be reached by automated download and the SIL site is behind an automated-access block

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing_statement (which is this very work, quoted from sec. 3.2) and compatible with the catalog's weight-sensitive kind: rightmost long vowel, else initial. It agrees with the catalog's Kondic 2012 South Eastern Huastec statement in kind (long vowel attracts stress, else first syllable) but note that Kondic's wording as carried in existing_statements is '(first) long vowel', whereas Hagberg/Larsen & Pike say the RIGHTMOST long vowel; the two differ only in words with two or more long vowels (Hagberg's hu:cu:k'cik, bi:noma:c, e:la:swa:y show final-long-vowel stress). Second-hand source; the empirical authority is Larsen & Pike 1949.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Unbounded quantity-sensitive stress: primary stress falls on the rightmost (last) long vowel of the word; if the word contains no long vowel, stress falls on the first vowel/syllable. Only vowel length counts as weight (the data show CVC syllables such as cabal, ?at'em, hilk'omac stressed initially, i.e. codas do not attract stress). Hagberg derives this without feet: Weight-to-Stress applied right-to-left plus End Rule Left, with the word as the stress domain. Data are second-hand, credited to Larsen & Pike 1949 (Potosino/ Veracruz-San Luis Potosí Huastec as described by Hayes 1981).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Huastec; the derivations mark a single stress per word and Hagberg notes that sequences of two stressless syllables occur wherever the long vowel places them (p. 47).
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. Hagberg states the pattern is exceptionless within the cited data; he notes (p. 47) that Hayes 1991 would need unbounded feet for these facts and rejects that analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Hagberg's data are Larsen & Pike 1949's Huastec (San Luis Potosí / Potosino variety, via Hayes 1981); the catalog's Kondic 2012 describes South Eastern Huastec; the supplementary Herrera Zendejas 2014 chapter describes the Huastec of Tancanhuitz, San Luis Potosí (consultant Amanda Zamora Ramírez). Herrera Zendejas 2011 (not obtained) presumably the same Tancanhuitz data.

readall_conflicts: One potential disagreement, not resolvable from the works opened here: Hagberg (after Hayes 1981 and Larsen & Pike 1949, Potosino Huastec) places stress on the RIGHTMOST long vowel, else the first syllable, whereas the catalog's first-hand source Kondic 2012 (South Eastern Huastec, as summarised in existing_statements) is reported as '(first) long vowel, else first short vowel'. These coincide for words with at most one long vowel and differ only for words with two or more long vowels (Hagberg's hu:cú:k'cik 'blisters', bi:nomá:c 'one who gave', e:la:swá:y). The supplementary Herrera Zendejas 2014 chapter (Tancanhuitz Huastec, pp. 274-280, not a listed work) gives only one-long-vowel words ('kuu.lab, 'laab.lij, pa.'t'aal, tsa.ma.'maal, wa.'k'aaʃ) plus initial stress in words without long vowels ('ka.le, 'ka.mab, 'pak.laθ), analysed as moraic trochees with codas weightless, and reports two primary stresses in -tal-aab abstract nouns ('hi.lij.ta.'laab), which she treats as two phonological words; that is compatible with both readings and adds the two-word domain detail. Herrera Zendejas 2011 could not be obtained, so whether it states 'rightmost' or 'leftmost' long vowel remains open.

sources.quote: "Como notaron Larsen y Pike (1949) para el huasteco de San Luis Potosí, el acento en huasteco de El Mamey, Tantoyuca, no es fonológico, es decir, es predecible mediante una regla: en palabras de dos o más sílabas, el acento recae en la sílaba que tiene un núcleo vocálico complejo. Cuando no hay longitud, el acento tiende a recaer en la primera sílaba a la izquierda de la palabra." Examples ['ʔat.em] 'sal', ['ʔol.om] 'cerdo', [ta.'jiːl] 'después', ['k'aː.mal], ['taː.ta], [ta.'taːʔ] 'tú'. (Veracruz/Tantoyuca variety; third variety now independently sourced.)

sources.quote: p.275: "Según los ejemplos de (a) ['ka.le, 'ka.mab, 'pak.laθ], el huasteco no distingue entre las sílabas CV y CVC para la asignación del acento ... las consonantes en coda no contribuyen al peso de la sílaba. El patrón acentual es fuerte-débil, por lo que corresponde a un patrón trocaico. En los ejemplos de (b) [pa.'t'aal, 'kuu.lab, tek'.'θaal, tsa.ma.'maal, wa.'k'aaʃ] apreciamos que la lengua es sensible a la cantidad, ya que si hay una sílaba con vocal larga, ésta atrae el acento." Analysed with moraic trochees; includes duration measurements (2 speakers) showing V: vs V contrast and coda s
